name: Prostamax
lead: Prostamax is a synthetic tetrapeptide with the sequence Lys-Glu-Asp-Pro (KEDP), developed by Russian gerontologist Vladimir Khavinson and colleagues at the St. Petersburg Institute of Bioregulation and Gerontology as one of a series of short-peptide "bioregulators" [1]. It was designed around the amino acid composition of Prostatilen, a prostate-tissue extract preparation, and is described by its developers as acting on prostate tissue [1].

Published work on Prostamax consists of cell-culture and animal experiments plus in vitro studies of lymphocytes from elderly donors, mostly from the Khavinson group and collaborators, reporting effects on chromatin structure [2][3][4]. No clinical trials were found. In looksmaxxing and longevity circles it appears as a niche "research peptide" in the same family as Epithalon.
infobox: V. Khavinson, St. Petersburg Institute of Bioregulation and Gerontology

paras: Proponents of the Khavinson bioregulator concept propose that short peptides enter cells and nuclei and interact with DNA and chromatin, altering gene expression [1][5]. For Prostamax, in vitro studies on lymphocytes from people aged about 75 to 88 report that the peptide caused decondensation of heterochromatin and activation of ribosomal genes [2][3][6]. These findings come from cultured cells, and their relevance to prostate function or appearance has not been tested in people.

In organ-culture experiments, a very low concentration of Prostamax and other synthetic peptides stimulated explants of prostate, heart, lung and pancreas tissue from young and old rats, according to the authors [4]. A separate study examined how Prostamax and copper or cadmium ions affected the thermal stability of chromatin in cultured lymphocytes from older people [7]. A general laboratory study found that several short peptides, including related Khavinson peptides, can enter HeLa cells and nuclei [5].
No studies found. Related work is limited to cell-culture and animal-tissue experiments, described above.

Prostamax is not approved as a medicine by major regulators and is sold in gray-market channels as a research chemical, according to the Grokipedia summary [1]. Little looksmaxxing-specific discussion could be sourced; its connection to appearance is indirect, via claimed anti-aging and prostate or hormonal support.

card.summary: A four-amino-acid Russian "bioregulator" peptide tied to prostate support; only cell and rat-tissue work exists.
card.note: No human trials; unregulated research-chemical product.

quick.overview:
Prostamax is a four-amino-acid peptide (Lys-Glu-Asp-Pro) from the Khavinson group in St. Petersburg, part of a family of short bioregulator peptides marketed for aging and organ-specific support. Its supposed target is the prostate.

Published work is limited to cultured cells and rat tissue, mostly from the developers' circle. No human trials were found, and its link to appearance is indirect.
quick.mechanism: Proponents propose that the peptide enters cell nuclei and loosens condensed chromatin, changing gene expression. This has been reported in lymphocytes from elderly donors in vitro.
quick.risks: No human safety data from trials were found. It has no regulatory approval for human use and is sold as a research chemical, so product purity is not assured.
